inputs.need:
I direct the internal medicine residency at a teaching hospital with 64 residents across three years. Since we moved to competency-based training two years ago, residents must collect workplace-based assessments of entrustable professional activities (EPAs) in an app: at least 12 per four-week rotation, each asking the supervisor for an entrustment rating and a short narrative comment. Our program evaluation committee is worried about assessment burden. The app export for last year shows that 38 percent of assessments were completed more than seven days after the observed activity, and the median narrative comment is nine words long. Residents tell us informally that they chase faculty at the end of the rotation and pick easy activities to hit the target, and some faculty say they complete batches of forms on Sunday evenings.

We do not know how residents and assessors actually experience this, which parts of the burden matter to them, or what they think the assessments are for. We plan a qualitative study with semi-structured interviews of residents and faculty assessors and focus groups with chief residents and program administrators, to understand how the EPA assessment workload is experienced and what drives late, thin or strategically chosen assessments. The findings will go to the competency committee before it revises the assessment targets next June.

I need help sharpening the question, choosing a sampling approach, deciding how many interviews are enough, and planning an analysis that the committee will trust. We have a part-time research assistant and no external funding.
inputs.constraints: No external funding. The research assistant is funded at 0.2 FTE until June 2027. Interviews must fit around clinical duties (lunch hours or the protected academic half-day). Individual residents' assessment records may not be viewed without their written consent.

records.title: Chasing signatures: a qualitative study of residents' experiences of entrustable professional activity assessment
records.authors: Okafor-Lindgren T, Brennan-Mwale S, Castillo-Hart R
records.abstract: Background: competency-based residency programmes require residents to collect workplace-based assessments of entrustable professional activities, but little is known about how residents experience the workload. Methods: we conducted semi-structured interviews with 24 residents in three internal medicine programmes and analysed the transcripts with reflexive thematic analysis. Results: residents described spending time chasing assessors at the end of rotations, choosing straightforward activities that supervisors were likely to observe, and treating the assessment target as an administrative quota. Several residents said they had stopped asking for assessments after difficult encounters because they feared a low rating would follow them. Conclusions: residents experienced assessment as a burden to be managed strategically; programmes should examine whether numerical targets undermine the formative purpose of assessment.

records.title: Assessors' accounts of entrustment decisions and narrative comments under clinical time pressure
records.abstract: We held focus groups with 31 faculty assessors in two academic hospitals to explore how they complete workplace-based assessments of entrustable professional activities. Assessors reported completing forms in batches, often days after the observed activity, and relying on memory of the resident rather than of the specific encounter. Many described writing brief narrative comments because they believed the comments were rarely read by anyone. Assessors valued a short conversation with the resident more than the form itself, and several said the form had replaced the conversation. The authors suggest that assessment design should reduce documentation time and make the feedback conversation, not the form, the unit of assessment.

records.title: Timeliness and narrative length of entrustable professional activity assessments: an analysis of mobile application records
records.authors: Mensah-Kowalski D, Fairbairn-Osei J, Tanaka-Ruiz P
records.abstract: We analysed 41,206 completed assessments of entrustable professional activities from a mobile assessment application used by 11 residency programmes over two academic years. The median delay between the observed activity and completion of the form was two days, and 29 percent of assessments were completed more than seven days later. Narrative comments on assessments completed after seven days were shorter (median 11 words) than comments on assessments completed on the same day (median 24 words). Entrustment ratings rose steadily through the year whatever the delay. Delay was greatest in the final week of each rotation. Timeliness may be a useful process marker of assessment quality, but these data cannot show why assessors delay.

records.title: Assessment burden in competency-based postgraduate medical education: a scoping review
records.authors: Delacroix-Mbeki A, Sorensen-Adeyemi F, Kaur-Whitfield N, Brandt-Oduya T
records.abstract: We mapped how assessment burden has been defined and studied in competency-based postgraduate training. We searched four bibliographic databases and included 46 reports published to 2020. Burden was most often described as time spent completing forms, but reports also described cognitive and emotional burden for residents and assessors and administrative burden for programmes. Only nine reports collected primary data from both residents and assessors, and none examined how burden changed after programmes altered their assessment targets. We found no agreed definition or measure of assessment burden. We recommend studies that include residents, assessors and programme administrators together and that describe the assessment system in enough detail for comparison.

records.title: Program directors' views on minimum numbers of workplace-based assessments per rotation: a national survey
records.abstract: We surveyed programme directors of internal medicine and family medicine residencies about the minimum number of workplace-based assessments they required per four-week rotation. Of 212 directors invited, 131 responded (62 percent). The median required number was 10 (range 4 to 20). Directors who set higher targets were more likely to report late or incomplete assessments, and 58 percent said that their targets had been chosen without evidence. Most directors wanted guidance on how many assessments are needed for a defensible competency decision. Responding directors may differ from those who did not respond, and the survey did not ask residents or assessors about their experience.

records.title: Tick-box culture: chief residents' perspectives on the purpose of competency assessment
records.abstract: Chief residents occupy a middle position between residents and faculty in assessment systems. We conducted three focus groups with 17 chief residents from five programmes. Participants described a tick-box culture in which the number of completed forms signalled engagement rather than learning. They reported that residents who were struggling were the least likely to request assessments, so the programme noticed their difficulties late. Chief residents proposed fewer and better assessments linked to direct observation and a regular coaching conversation. The study predates the full introduction of entrustable professional activities in the participating programmes, and the chief residents were selected by their programme directors.

records.title: Reducing required assessments from twelve to eight per rotation: effect on narrative comment quality in one residency programme
records.authors: Fitzgerald-Onu C, Park-Hallstrom I, Moreau-Ansah G
records.abstract: One internal medicine programme reduced its minimum number of entrustable professional activity assessments from twelve to eight per four-week rotation. We compared assessments from the year before and the year after the change. Two raters blinded to the period scored 600 sampled narrative comments with a structured quality rubric. The proportion of comments rated as specific and actionable rose from 34 percent to 47 percent, and the median comment length increased from 12 to 19 words. The total number of assessments fell by 28 percent. Progression decisions made by the competency committee were unchanged. The comparison is uncontrolled, and faculty development sessions on feedback were also introduced in the same year.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Two qualitative studies describe residents managing assessment targets strategically (chasing assessors, choosing easy activities) and assessors completing forms late and in batches from memory. A large log analysis links delayed completion with shorter comments, and an uncontrolled before-after report suggests that a lower target improved comment quality. A scoping review finds no agreed definition of assessment burden and few studies that ask residents, assessors and administrators together. The evidence supports a qualitative study across roles in this programme; it does not settle what the target should be.
response.gradeRationale: Mostly single-site qualitative studies and uncontrolled comparisons; consistent in direction on strategic and delayed assessment, but transferability to this programme is uncertain and no study measured burden before and after a change in targets.

response.reading: The target of 12 assessments per rotation sits between two groups with different workloads: residents who must request and collect assessments, and assessors who must observe, rate and write. The retrieved studies connect the target to strategic requesting by residents (c1) and to late, memory-based completion by assessors (c5), and link delay to thinner comments (c2). Chief residents and administrators see the system from the middle and the edge, and struggling residents may request the fewest assessments. The committee's June decision depends on understanding these mechanisms, which the app export alone cannot show.

store.title: Residents' and assessors' experience of entrustable professional activity assessment burden in an internal medicine residency

includes: Residents' and assessors' experience of entrustable professional activity assessment burden in an internal medicine residency

response.overview: Qualitative study in one internal medicine residency from October 2026 to March 2027: semi-structured interviews with residents and faculty assessors, and focus groups with chief residents and programme administrators, analysed with reflexive thematic analysis; findings reported to the competency committee in May 2027.
response.population: Residents in training years 1 to 3 (purposive sample across years, gender, international and local graduates, and low and high assessment counts), faculty assessors across inpatient and clinic rotations, the three chief residents, and the four programme administrators. Residents with pending remediation decisions are not approached during those months.
response.exposure: The EPA assessment system as experienced: the target of 12 app-based assessments per rotation, entrustment ratings and narrative comments.
response.procedures: The research assistant, who has no role in progression decisions, sends invitations through the residents' association and the department office. Interviews (45 to 60 minutes, in person or by video, in lunch hours) follow a guide covering the last rotation, how assessments were requested and completed, what they were for, and what should change; the guide is piloted with one resident and one assessor who are not included. Two focus groups (chief residents; administrators) run in the protected half-day. Recordings are transcribed verbatim and de-identified before the programme director sees any transcript. Two analysts code independently at first, then meet to develop themes, keeping a reflexive log.

outcomes.why: Gives the committee options grounded in participants' reasons, without claiming effects.

outcomes.why: Shows why sampling stopped and who is represented.

outcomes.timing: At each interview and focus group

parsimony.simplestPath: Interviews and two focus groups in one programme, one thematic analysis, one report to the committee.

response.theoreticalFramework: None imposed in advance; reflexive thematic analysis with an inductive orientation, using the scoping review's distinction between time, cognitive, emotional and administrative burden only as a sensitising device.
response.summary: Interviews and focus groups across four roles, one primary thematic outcome, a secondary set of proposals, and process and balancing measures.

response.designSummary: Qualitative interviews and focus groups analysed with reflexive thematic analysis; no statistical testing.
response.sampleSize: Sample size is set by information power rather than a power calculation. The aim is narrow, participants hold dense and specific experience of one system, the analysis is applied, and the interviewer can sustain good dialogue; together these suggest about 14 to 18 interviews (8 to 10 residents across the three years and 6 to 8 assessors) plus two focus groups of 3 to 6 people. Information power is judged and recorded after every fourth interview; the research assistant's 0.2 FTE sets a ceiling of 22 interviews before March 2027.
response.primaryAnalysis: Reflexive thematic analysis in six phases: familiarisation, coding, generating initial themes, reviewing, defining and naming, and writing up. Two analysts code the first four transcripts independently, discuss differences as interpretive resources rather than errors, and one analyst continues coding with regular review. Themes are developed across roles and then examined for differences by role and training year.
response.secondaryAnalysis: A framework matrix sets participants' proposals for changing targets against their roles and reasons. The app export (delay and comment length by rotation) is summarised descriptively to describe the setting, not linked to individual participants.
response.missingData: A participant who withdraws before analysis has the transcript removed; partial interviews are analysed for what they contain. The number of residents invited, declining and taking part is reported by assessment count group.
response.multiplicity: Not applicable: no hypothesis tests. Themes are reported with the range of roles that support them, not with counts presented as strength of evidence.
response.software: University-licensed qualitative data management software for coding; transcripts stored on the university research drive.
overfittingGuards: Interview guide fixed before the first interview except for documented probes
Reflexive log kept by both analysts from the first transcript
Negative cases sought for every candidate theme
No participant counts presented as evidence of theme strength
response.summary: Information power suggests 14 to 18 interviews and two focus groups, reviewed every fourth interview; reflexive thematic analysis across roles.

response.risks: Minimal physical risk. The main risks are that residents fear consequences for criticising the programme, that assessors feel judged, and that small groups make individuals identifiable in quotations.
response.consent: Written informed consent before each interview and focus group, taken by the research assistant; participants may withdraw until analysis begins, and declining has no effect on assessments or progression.
response.data: Audio recordings deleted after verified transcription; transcripts de-identified (names, rotations, dates removed) and stored on the university research drive with access limited to the two analysts; quotations checked for identifiability before any report.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: residents who are international medical graduates, those with caring responsibilities, part-time residents and residents with low assessment counts may experience the target differently and may be least likely to volunteer. Invitations are made through the residents' association as well as the department office, sampling is purposive across these groups, and the report states which groups are thinly represented.
response.effectiveness: The study is useful if it gives the committee reasons and mechanisms it can act on in June; it will not claim that any change to the target works.
response.efficiency: Uses existing research assistant time and approved half-days; interviews in lunch hours avoid lost clinical time.
response.costs: Staff time only: about 180 hours of research assistant time and 40 hours of analyst time; no transcription service fee because transcription is done in house.
response.grants: None needed; a departmental education research award could fund dissemination to other programmes.
response.partnerships: Residents' association (recruitment and guide review), a faculty assessor representative, the chief residents, and the programme administrators.
response.rebPath: Approved by the hospital research ethics board as minimal-risk research (approval REB-2026-0412, 2026-09-03). Any change to the interview guide beyond probes is submitted as an amendment.
response.limitations: One programme; findings are transferable by description, not generalisable by sampling; participants may shape accounts for an audience that includes their programme.
response.summary: Minimal-risk study with written consent, an independent interviewer, de-identified transcripts and purposive sampling of residents least likely to volunteer.

response.partnershipPlan: Two residents nominated by the residents' association and one faculty assessor review the interview guide before piloting and read the draft themes for recognisability before the committee report.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; anonymous comments from the last two annual resident surveys about assessment are read to sensitise the guide.

items.theme: The quota at the end of the rotation
items.quote: Composite paraphrase (resident): In the last week I stop learning and start collecting; I send the same request to four people and hope two answer.
items.implication: Ask about the timing of requests across the rotation, not only the total.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase (assessor): The useful part was the two minutes at the bedside; the form comes a week later and says less.
items.implication: Explore whether the form could record the conversation rather than replace it.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase (resident): After a bad night I would never ask for an assessment on that case, even though that is where I needed feedback.
items.implication: Probe for avoided assessments and what would make them safe to request.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase (programme administrator): I send reminders about numbers every Friday; nobody asks me whether the comments say anything.
items.implication: Include administrators, whose monitoring may reinforce the quota.

response.summary: Four composite voices on end-of-rotation collecting, lost conversations, avoided assessments and quota monitoring.

response.title: Experiences of entrustable professional activity assessment workload among residents, assessors and administrators: a qualitative study in an internal medicine residency
response.abstract: Purpose: to understand how residents, faculty assessors, chief residents and administrators experience the workload of EPA assessment and why assessments are late, brief or strategically chosen. Method: semi-structured interviews and two focus groups, October 2026 to March 2027, analysed with reflexive thematic analysis. Results and conclusions will be written after analysis.
response.introduction: Competency-based residencies rely on frequent workplace-based assessment, and programmes set minimum numbers without agreed evidence. Retrieved studies describe residents managing targets strategically and assessors completing forms late from memory, but few studies ask residents, assessors and administrators together.
response.methods: Purposive sampling across training years, graduate background and assessment counts; interviews by a research assistant without a progression role; focus groups in protected time; reflexive thematic analysis by two analysts with a reflexive log. Ethics approval REB-2026-0412.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present themes with supporting quotations by role, a table of participants by role and training year, and participants' proposals for the assessment target.
response.discussion: The discussion will relate the themes to the retrieved accounts of strategic requesting and late completion, consider what they imply for the June target review, and state what a single-programme study cannot show.
response.limitations: One programme; accounts may be shaped by the programme audience; residents with the most difficult experiences may be under-represented.
response.conclusion: To be written after analysis; it will describe mechanisms and proposals and will not claim that any target change works.
response.summary: COREQ-structured draft with results left empty until analysis.

path.problem.rawNeed:
I direct the internal medicine residency at a teaching hospital with 64 residents across three years. Since we moved to competency-based training two years ago, residents must collect workplace-based assessments of entrustable professional activities (EPAs) in an app: at least 12 per four-week rotation, each asking the supervisor for an entrustment rating and a short narrative comment. Our program evaluation committee is worried about assessment burden. The app export for last year shows that 38 percent of assessments were completed more than seven days after the observed activity, and the median narrative comment is nine words long. Residents tell us informally that they chase faculty at the end of the rotation and pick easy activities to hit the target, and some faculty say they complete batches of forms on Sunday evenings.

We do not know how residents and assessors actually experience this, which parts of the burden matter to them, or what they think the assessments are for. We plan a qualitative study with semi-structured interviews of residents and faculty assessors and focus groups with chief residents and program administrators, to understand how the EPA assessment workload is experienced and what drives late, thin or strategically chosen assessments. The findings will go to the competency committee before it revises the assessment targets next June.

I need help sharpening the question, choosing a sampling approach, deciding how many interviews are enough, and planning an analysis that the committee will trust. We have a part-time research assistant and no external funding.
path.problem.constraints: No external funding. The research assistant is funded at 0.2 FTE until June 2027. Interviews must fit around clinical duties (lunch hours or the protected academic half-day). Individual residents' assessment records may not be viewed without their written consent.
